name: Union-Find and Connected Components
intent: Answer 'are these two things in the same group?' while groups keep merging, using a forest of parent pointers kept shallow by union by rank and path compression, and know when a plain graph traversal is the simpler tool.
scenario: A service receives a stream of 'these two accounts belong together' edges for 1,000 elements and must answer 'are 0 and the newest connected?' after every edge. A naive parent-pointer structure needs 500,499 pointer operations because the trees turn into one long chain; adding union by rank and path compression brings it to 3,993. A team that re-runs a graph traversal after every edge needs 1,499,499, but on a fixed graph one traversal pass would have done the job in 5,000.
problem: Connectivity questions come up everywhere: which accounts are the same person, which pixels form one blob, which cities are linked by the roads built so far, whether adding this edge creates a cycle in a minimum spanning tree. A traversal answers them once, but a graph that keeps growing makes you start over after every change. The trap with the cheap structure that fixes this is that its simplest form degrades to a linked list, and the fix is two small rules that are easy to forget or to apply in a way that does nothing.

howItWorks.title: Every group is a tree of parent pointers
howItWorks.text: Start with each element as its own group: parent[x] = x. The group's representative is the root, the element that is its own parent. find(x) follows parent pointers until it reaches the root; two elements are in the same group exactly when their roots are equal. union(a, b) finds both roots and, if they differ, makes one root the parent of the other. Nothing stores the list of members: the group is implied by the pointers, which is why merging is so cheap.

howItWorks.title: Why the plain version goes wrong
howItWorks.text: A union that always hangs one root under the other can build a chain: joining 0-1, 1-2, 2-3 and so on leaves a path n elements long, and every find(0) walks all of it. In the chain workload with 1,000 elements and a question after every edge, that is 500,499 pointer steps, roughly n squared over two. With random edges the trees stay lower but still reach a depth of 87 at 1,000 elements, and 109,799 operations in total. Correctness is never in doubt; only the cost is.

howItWorks.title: Union by rank: attach the shallower tree under the deeper one
howItWorks.text: Keep a rank per root, an upper bound on its tree height, and when merging hang the root with the smaller rank under the other; on a tie pick either and raise the winner's rank by one. A tree reaches rank k only by merging two of rank k - 1, so it needs at least 2 to the power k elements, and the height is at most log2 of the number of elements. Random edges now give a deepest path of 5 instead of 87. Union by size (attach the smaller group) gives the same guarantee and is just as common.

howItWorks.title: Path compression: flatten while you look
howItWorks.text: While find walks from x to the root, it can then point every node on that path straight at the root. The first find is no cheaper, but the next find through any of those nodes takes one step. On the chain workload, compression alone needs 3,994 operations instead of 500,499. Compression changes the structure during a read, so it makes find a writer: that matters for thread safety, because two threads calling find at once now race on the parent array.

howItWorks.title: Together they are close to constant, and they have limits
howItWorks.text: With both rules, a sequence of operations costs close to one pointer step each: 4,777 operations for 1,000 random edges and 1,000 questions, against 109,799 plain. The textbook bound is amortized O(alpha(n)) per operation, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, which stays below 5 for any input that fits in a computer. But union-find only merges: it cannot split a group or remove an edge, it cannot tell you the path between two elements, and a traversal of the finished graph is just as good when the edges never change (5,000 operations in one pass).

pros: Close to constant time per union or connectivity question once both rules are in place, even for millions of elements
Handles edges that arrive over time, which a one-shot traversal cannot without starting over
Tiny: two integer arrays and a few lines of code
Cycle detection while adding edges comes for free: an edge whose endpoints already share a root closes a cycle (the core of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree)
cons: Merge only: a deleted edge or a split group is not supported, so the structure suits growing graphs, not changing ones
Stores group membership implicitly: listing the members or finding a path needs extra bookkeeping or another structure
Path compression turns reads into writes, which complicates concurrent use and persistence
The first rule you skip degrades silently to a chain: results stay correct and only the speed collapses
whenToUse: Edges or merge facts arrive over time and you must answer connectivity questions between them
Grouping duplicates or equivalent records, such as accounts, entities or equivalent variables in a type checker
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, and image or grid labelling where regions merge as you scan
You only need 'same group or not' and the group count, never the members in order
whenNotToUse: The graph is fixed or you ask only once: one breadth-first or depth-first pass labels every component in n plus edges steps, with no extra structure
Edges are also removed (links go down, friendships end): union-find cannot undo a merge, so use a structure built for deletions, an offline method that replays updates, or recompute
You need the actual path, the shortest path or the distances between elements, which connectivity alone does not give
The data is distributed across machines and the groups must be agreed on by everyone: a single shared array is the wrong shape, and the problem is a coordination one
pitfalls: Implementing find without compression and union without rank, then testing on random data: it looks fine (deepest path 87 at 1,000 elements) and collapses on sorted or chain-like input, where 1,000 edges cost 500,499 operations
Applying compression in a union function that compares elements instead of roots, or forgetting to find the roots before linking: linking two non-roots corrupts the groups silently
Keeping the rank and forgetting that compression makes it an upper bound, not an exact height: do not 'fix' ranks after compression, the guarantee still holds
Reaching for union-find when the graph never changes: a single traversal does the job in 5,000 steps with no structure to maintain, and is easier to read and to debug
Re-running a traversal after every new edge on a growing graph: on the chain workload that is 1,499,499 operations, three times worse than the plain union-find it was meant to replace
Expecting deletions: removing a link needs a different structure; some designs keep the merge history and roll it back in reverse order, which allows undo but not deleting an arbitrary old edge

Calling find from several threads without thinking: with compression it writes, so concurrent finds can race; use a lock, a lock-free variant written for that, or compress only in a single-writer phase

quiz.question: With 1,000 elements and a question after every edge, plain union-find costs 500,499 operations. What produces that growth?
options: The trees become a long chain, so every find walks a path that grows with each edge.
Each union copies one group's members into the other group's list.
Random edges create many separate groups that all have to be searched.
The parent array is resized every time two groups merge.
quiz.explanation: Hanging one root under another with no rule can build a path through all the elements, and each find(0) walks it: about n squared over two steps in total. Union by rank or path compression cuts it to about 4,000 because the path stays short.

quiz.question: A graph is built once and never changes. You need the component count and answers to 1,000 'are these connected?' questions. What is the simplest good choice?
options: Union-find with rank only, because traversals are always slower.
A traversal that labels every component once, then compares labels.
Re-run a depth-first search for each question from the first element.
A balanced tree keyed by element number.
quiz.explanation: One pass over the fixed graph costs about n plus the edges (5,000 operations for 1,000 elements and 1,000 edges), and each question is a label comparison. Union-find costs about the same there, so its extra machinery buys nothing.

quiz.question: Which request can union-find, as described here, NOT handle?
options: Telling whether two elements are in the same group.
Counting how many groups exist after many merges.
Detecting that a new edge would close a cycle.
Removing an old edge and splitting its group back in two.
quiz.explanation: Merging is irreversible in the parent forest: nothing records which edge joined what, and path compression has erased the original shape. Deletions need structures built for them, or replaying the edges that remain.
